results.title: Self-Hosting an LLM: Is It Actually Cheaper Than the API?
highlights:
Start with the optimistic number, because it's the one that gets quoted. Take an H100 at $2.89/hr on-demand (RunPod Secure Cloud H100 PCIe, unchanged as of September 27, 2026), serving gpt-oss-120b (the current single-GPU workhorse, a 120B MoE that fits one 80GB card at its native MXFP4 precision) at a benchmarked aggregate throughput of ~8,000 tokens/second per GPU on a realistic mixed workload (GPUStack, vLLM). That's about 28.8 million tokens per hour, so the raw GPU cost is roughly $0.10 per million tokens at full saturation. Next to GPT-5.5 at $30 per million output tokens, that looks like a 300× saving. That single comparison is how most "just self-host it" arguments get built. The comparison that matters: Groq, Fireworks, and Together all serve the identical gpt-oss-120b for $0.60 per million output tokens, and DeepInfra's base endpoint lists $0.17, so at perfect utilization your raw margin over just calling the hosted model is about 6×, before you've paid anyone to run it. (You'll also see wilder self-hosting multiples in the wild; they usually come from dividing an hourly rate by a single-stream token count, or a straight arithmetic slip.)

...

Raw GPU rental only. Multiply by the 3–5× ops factor for all-in cost. Derived from RunPod on-demand rates (H100 PCIe Secure Cloud $2.89/hr, H200 Community Cloud $3.59/hr, both unchanged as of September 27, 2026) and DeepInfra list prices (pulled July 22, 2026), GPUStack's vLLM benchmark for gpt-oss-120b on H100, and the vLLM project's production figure of 2,200 tok/s per H200 for 671B-class DeepSeek (8-GPU minimum; per-GPU shown). Throughputs are aggregate served tokens on batched workloads. Read the last column carefully: for the 671B MoE, the hosted API beats your raw GPU cost at every utilization level, and even for gpt-oss-120b, all-in cost with ops beats the $0.60 hosted price only above roughly 50–80% sustained utilization.

...

results.title: Compute Is Becoming a Tradable Commodity — and Wall Street Is Racing to Build the Market — On The Wire
highlights:
Compute futures apply that idea to renting GPUs — the chips that train and run AI models. And the problem they're built to solve is real. According to the research firm SemiAnalysis, the price of renting an Nvidia H100 on a one-year contract climbed nearly 40% in five months, from a low of around $1.70 per hour in October 2025 to roughly $2.35 by March 2026. Spot prices swing even more wildly — depending on the provider and how long you commit, an H100 today can cost anywhere from about $1.50 to over $11 an hour, with the market median somewhere near $3.

...

CME and Silicon Data will base their contracts on Silicon Data's "Silicon Index," a daily benchmark of H100 and A100 rental rates captured across cloud providers and recalculated every business day. Silicon Data is backed by the trading firm DRW, whose founder Don Wilson predicts "compute will become the largest commodity in the world." The contracts are expected to be cash-settled to that index, with a launch planned for later this year pending regulatory review.

ICE and Ornn take a different tack. Their contracts reference the Ornn Compute Price Index, which Ornn says is the first compute benchmark built only from printed transactions — actual executed trades, rather than surveyed rates. The contracts are dollar-denominated and cash-settled, and would cover a wider spread of chips: H100, H200, B200 and even the RTX 5090. The survey-based-versus-transaction-based distinction is the crux of a genuine debate about which method better reflects the true price of compute.

H2 — H100 Market Segmentation: A Two-Tier Dynamic Threatening Neocloud Margins at the Margin Confidence: 3 / 5

Thesis: The original framing of an H100 "stealth price war" is too clean. What the data actually reveals is a structurally segmented H100 SPOT market with three distinct tiers: a surplus/offload tier (Iowa at $1.24/hr median with a near-8,800% spread between its floor and ceiling — one provider is effectively clearing near zero), a demand-driven mid-market tier (Virginia at $2.71/hr, +5.6% over 30 days, actually rising), and a premium/constrained tier (California at $5.16/hr, +29.4%; Japan at $8.81–$10.93/hr, frozen). The investable risk is not that H100 pricing is uniformly collapsing — Virginia and California contradict that — but that the existence of an Iowa-tier surplus market creates an arbitrage channel: enterprise customers with workload flexibility are now able to access H100 capacity at $1.24/hr in Iowa when they may be paying $7–10/hr on contracted rates elsewhere. This two-tier dynamic doesn't break neocloud revenue today, but it seeds the conditions for contract renegotiation at renewal — particularly as customers grow more sophisticated about spot market availability. The CoreWeave gross margin trajectory makes this threat concrete and observable: gross margin has declined from 74.2% in Q2 2025 to 65.5% in Q1 2026, a compression of 870 basis points across three consecutive quarters. This is not a one-off; it is a trend. EPS misses of −22%, −30%, and −22% in the last three consecutive reported quarters suggest cost structures are not scaling as efficiently as the revenue ramp.

Key Evidence:

1. H100 SPOT Iowa: $1.24/hr median, min $0.028/hr, max $2.45/hr — near-8,800% spread indicating one provider in aggressive clearance (live ticker data, June 21, 2026)
2. H100 SPOT Virginia: $2.71/hr, +5.6% over 30d — CRWV's home market is tightening, not collapsing; contradicts uniform-price-war framing (live ticker data, June 21, 2026)
3. H100 ON_DEMAND Virginia: $8.69/hr, essentially flat (−0.02% over 30d) — hyperscalers have not flinched on list prices; enterprise contract pricing remains sticky (live ticker data, June 21, 2026)
4. CRWV gross margin: 74.2% (Q2 2025) → 71.0% (Q3 2025) → 67.6% (Q4 2025) → 65.5% (Q1 2026) — 870 bps compression in three quarters; trend is the signal (CRWV 10-Q, Q1 2026)
5. CRWV EPS misses: −22% (May 2026), −30% (February 2026), −22% (prior quarter) — three consecutive misses confirming cost inefficiency relative to revenue ramp (earnings data, June 2026)
6. CRWV current ratio: 0.315 — critically illiquid against $35.1B total debt; $2.27B cash vs. near-term liabilities (CRWV fundamentals, June 2026)
7. CRWV two unscraped 8-Ks filed June 18 (EX-4.1) and May 18 (EX-10.1) — high probability debt instrument filings given capital structure (SEC EDGAR, June 18, 2026)
8. Qualifying counterpoint: CRWV Q1 2026 revenue $2.08B (+112% YoY, +32% QoQ); operating cash flow $2.98B in Q1 alone — the underlying business model generates cash before capex. Revenue trajectory is exceptional; the risk is margin, not viability.

results.title: Neocloud, Decoded
highlights:
Open LinkedIn on any given day and you'll see “neocloud” attached to Anthropic, Vultr, Nebius, CoreWeave, and half a dozen other companies. The word has become shorthand for “something to do with AI and data centers,” which is exactly the problem — these are different businesses, with different customers and very different risk profiles.

...

## Three Different Businesses, One Word 

 “Neocloud” gets stretched across three things that are actually quite different: 

### 1. Infrastructure operators — the actual neoclouds

 CoreWeave, Nebius, Vultr, IREN, Crusoe, Lambda. These companies build or lease GPU-dense data centers and sell computing power by the hour, or under long-term contract. This is the only group that really fits the neocloud label. 

### 2. AI labs — buyers, not sellers

 Anthropic and OpenAI sit here. They're customers of computing power, not vendors of it. Anthropic trains and runs its Claude models across AWS, Google, and NVIDIA hardware — renting capacity rather than reselling it. 

### 3. Hyperscalers — the original full-stack clouds

 AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure remain the broad, general-purpose platforms with decades of enterprise trust behind them. Increasingly, they're also investors in — and customers of — both groups above, which is where this gets genuinely interesting.

...

## The Other Half of the Pitch: Lower Cost 

 Beyond speed, neoclouds also tend to be meaningfully cheaper for raw GPU access, because they aren't carrying the cost of hundreds of bundled enterprise services the way a hyperscaler does. One widely cited industry comparison shows the gap: 

 Figure 1. Hyperscaler pricing reflects the cost of a much broader service catalog; neoclouds strip that down to a single, transparent rate. 

 A few reasons the gap exists: 

 • Smaller, focused catalog — raw compute and fast networking, instead of hundreds of bundled services. 

 • Simple, transparent pricing — one rate per GPU-hour, without the surprise fees that make hyperscaler bills hard to predict. 

 • Newer hardware, sooner — a smaller catalog means new chip generations reach customers faster.

How the pricing works, in full

Charges accrue by the minute against a prepaid balance (minimum top-up $5, unused credit refundable), and prices are identical in every region. CPU sizes run from small (1 vCPU, 1 GB) at $0.013/hr to 6xl (60 vCPU, 240 GB, 900 GB) at $3.714/hr. The three -nvme sizes cost about 17% more per hour for NVMe storage, and the two -premium sizes (xl-premium $0.236/hr, xxl-premium $0.473/hr) use dedicated vCPUs. GPU sizes run from gpu-4000ada-1 at $0.836/hr to gpu-h200-8 (8x H200) at $39.336/hr; the MI300X, H100 and H200 rates rose on 1 August 2026 after DigitalOcean raised its own GPU prices. A suspended machine pays only $0.078/GB/month for image storage. There is no free tier. Rates read from machine0.io on 2026-10-19.

...

The product has moved quickly since the June listing. The changelog records a US West region on 10 July 2026, NVMe sizes the same day, dedicated-vCPU premium sizes on 2 August, published GPU rates that rose on 1 August after DigitalOcean raised its own, a TypeScript SDK on 12 October, standing orders for out-of-stock sizes on 13 October and scheduled actions, still experimental, on 15 October. The same changelog admits that GPU sizes were wrongly shown as out of stock from 25 August until a fix on 12 October, so check capacity before planning around a size. GPU sizes are offered in four of the five regions; US West is CPU only.
